title: A Space Shuttle Engineer Looks at the King's Chamber
description:
Moving something enormous is only half the job. The other half is setting it exactly where it belongs.

Travis Robinson grew up fixing tractors on a Texas farm, then worked as a mechanical engineer on the Space Shuttle program with Rockwell International. In this Ancient Atlas conversation, he brings his experience with training hardware, systems integration, and careful Shuttle assembly to the granite of the Great Pyramid's King's Chamber.

How do you place something immense with precision? And what happens if you need to move it again?

title: The Paracas Candelabra & Islas Ballestas · A Boat Trip Off Peru in 4K
description:
A giant figure cut into the desert hillside, facing the sea. Then islands so crowded with seabirds the rock turns white.

The Paracas Candelabra is about 180 metres tall and faces the sea. Who made it, and when, is still debated. Beyond it lie the Islas Ballestas, part of Peru's Guano Islands reserve: Peruvian pelicans, cormorants and boobies by the thousand, and South American sea lions hauled out on the rocks. The white is guano, once the country's most valuable export.

No narration. Just the boat, the water and the islands.

description:
We started with one video from China and a healthy dose of doubt. title: Moray · A Slow Walk Through the Inca Circles of Peru's Sacred Valley (4K)
description:
Rings within rings, cut into the earth.

Moray sits on a high plateau in Peru's Sacred Valley, about 3,500 metres up, near the village of Maras. The Inca shaped these hollows into terraced circles, the largest about 30 metres deep. The bowl holds its own climate: sun, wind and cold air settle differently on every ring, and the floor can be far cooler than the rim. Many believe the Inca used it to learn how crops grow at different heights.

Let your breathing slow to the pace of the walk. Notice the curve of each terrace as it turns, the wind in the dry grass, the quiet at the bottom of the bowl.

As the circles draw you in, you might find yourself coming back here whenever you need somewhere still to go. Deep Horizon is a place for that: one ancient site at a time, slowly.

title: You Know More Than You Think
description:
To understand the past, we first have to understand how we know anything is true.

Gerald, Cody and Jeff sit down with a question that sits underneath every ancient site we visit: what does it actually mean to know something? You'll find five ways of knowing you already use every day (your gut, your senses, your reasoning, trusted sources, and what works in practice) and how each one sharpens the others, like strings on the same guitar. By the end, a megalithic wall, a starry sky or a bold claim online will all look a little different.

No experts required. Just curiosity, and the confidence to look again.

title: Sillustani · A Slow Walk to the Towers Above Lake Umayo, Peru
description:
You've seen the famous places. This is the quiet one.

Sillustani sits on a peninsula in Lake Umayo, in southern Peru, about 3,900 metres up. The stone towers are chullpas: built before and during the Inca period. Most of them face east, toward the sunrise.

Let your shoulders drop. Follow the path at walking pace. Notice the wind in the grass, the light on the stone, the lake opening up at the end.

As you settle in, you might find you want to come back here. Deep Horizon is a place for that: one ancient site at a time, slowly, whenever you need somewhere quiet to go.

title: Inside Qorikancha, the Inca Temple Under a Church · Brien Foerster & Jimmy Church
description:
Qorikancha was the centre of the Inca world. The Spanish took its gold, built a church on top of it, and plastered over the walls. In 1950 an earthquake brought the church down. The stone underneath held.

Brien Foerster and Jimmy Church walk you through it: the joints, the walls that lean on purpose, the room that rings, the gold that was there, and the shaft under the courtyard that Brien says leads to a tunnel running to Sacsayhuamán.

Look at the stone with them, then decide for yourself.

title: Why Do Ancient Cities End Up Underground?
description:
Cities are built on top of cities. Roads sink into the rock. And everywhere people pass, someone leaves a mark.

Three friends trace what lies beneath our feet: Troy's stacked cities, a Cusco street sitting on Inca and older stonework, a mosque built over Luxor Temple, plague burials found under London, an English lane worn deep into the hillside by centuries of feet and carts, and the names people have scratched into stone from Pompeii to Dendera to Hagia Sophia.

title: Hidden on Purpose: The Chamber Under Dendera
description:
At the Temple of Hathor at Dendera there is a chamber that was hidden twice. As Ben and Russ described it, the way down sat under two false floors: lift the paving and you find what looks like solid foundation, and anyone digging would have stopped there. The room is below that.

We went down. It is tight enough that your backpack gets stuck, and the walls are covered, floor to ceiling, in some of the most famous and argued-over carvings in Egypt.

Egyptologists read the best-known scene as a lotus giving birth to a serpent, held up by a djed pillar with arms: a creation image. Other people look at the same wall and see something electrical. The room itself does not settle it, and neither do we. What it does settle is that someone went to a great deal of trouble to put this writing exactly here, and then to hide it.

Part three of our conversation with Brent Slava. Part one is the Scablands, part two is where all the stone went.

title: Where Did All the Stone Go?
description:
Abu Simbel was never built. It was cut into a cliff, which means the temple and the mountain were one piece of stone with no joints anywhere in it. To move it out of the way of the High Dam, engineers had to run that backwards: turn a subtraction into an assembly, by sawing a single monolith into 1,047 numbered blocks.

That is the part everyone tells you. Here is the part nobody does.

Cut a temple out of a mountain and you are left holding the mountain. Hundreds of thousands of tons of it. Lalibela, Kailasa and Abu Simbel are not defined by what is standing. They are defined by what is missing, and there is no spoil heap anywhere to account for it.

We wanted a control, so we found one, and it is embarrassing. In 2012 Los Angeles moved a single uncut boulder about sixty miles to sit outside an art museum. Three hundred and forty tons. One rock. It took years, it cost roughly ten million dollars, and it needed a custom transporter longer than a blue whale travelling at two miles an hour under police escort.

One rock. Now look at Lalibela again.

Part two of our conversation with Brent Slava. Part one is the Scablands (https://youtu.be/0rwtMIIRmg8).

title: Nepal Lost a Whole Valley in 24 Hours. That Was the Teardrop.
description:
A flood came down on the Rasuwagadhi border crossing between Nepal and China and took it off the map. Not over a week. In twenty-four hours. We watched the before and after from orbit, and Gerald said the thing that set off everything after it: by comparison, that was just a teardrop.

So we went looking for what he was comparing it to. Eastern Washington, where something moved seventeen million cubic metres of water every second and left the basalt stripped bare behind it. Dry Falls, a cataract several times the width of Niagara that ran dry. A drive that takes four hours today, undone in an afternoon.

Then it stops being about water and becomes about ice. How much liquid water sits under a polar cap. What the crust does when you take a mile of weight off it quickly. And why the Great Lakes are tipping toward Detroit while people on both shores are each certain the other side is misreading the water.

It ends on Niagara, which turns out to have a birthday, worked out from shells in the gorge, and which is slowly reversing into the lake that made it.

title: Angkor Wat's Dating Problem, with Solstice Hunter
description:
The Solstice Hunter has photographed polygonal and L-shaped blockwork across 71 Cambodian temple sites. Nobody else is documenting them. In most cases her footage is the first look anyone outside Cambodia has had at a particular wall.

The through-line is attribution rather than dating. Bayon carves daily life, hunting and
war in exhaustive detail and carves nobody building anything. When a Chinese envoy reached
Angkor in 1296 and asked, he was told the temple was the grave of Lu Ban, a Chinese god of
architecture. Whatever the dates turn out to be, the record does not name a builder.

Nobody in this conversation is an archaeologist. That is said out loud in the first minute
and it is the point: the argument is made from photographs, tool marks and primary
accounts, and where the evidence runs out we say so rather than filling the gap.

title: Half of Machu Picchu Is Underground · with Brien Foerster
description:
Half of Machu Picchu is underground.

Not the terraces, not the temples. The water system. Once you are told that, the whole site reads differently: the terracing is drainage, the stone
channels are drainage, and the reason the Inca refused to build at river
level is that they had already watched the river do what it did in 2010.

Brien Foerster has spent twenty years on these sites, and this is one
afternoon of one of his tours. He is a creator on the Ancient Atlas.

Three kinds of work sit on the same eight-thousand-foot saddle here: rock cut back where it stood, megalithic blocks set dry, and coursed fieldstone laid later. The interesting question is not which came first. It is why anyone would build all three in one place.

title: Every Block Was Placed By Hand. About 2.3 Million of Them.
description:
Brent Slava came back from Egypt with something he couldn't prove.

So we tested it. We spent an afternoon zoomed into a single carved eye, the one you've seen on a thousand tea towels, and found a working fraction system hiding inside it. Every stroke doing two jobs, on a symbol so common nobody looks twice.

Then we argued about whether you can feel that through a screen, or whether you have to stand in the room and put your hand on it.

You can force people to move stone. Nobody has ever been forced to care. That turns out to be the whole difference, and it's why something made four and a half thousand years ago can still reach you, and why you can tell in about a second when something wasn't.

title: 200 Underground Cities. Nobody Left a Chisel.
description:
Two hundred underground cities under Cappadocia alone. So where are all the chisels?

Cappadocia has more than two hundred of them. So does Georgia. So does China, and India, and Italy. People who never met, on separate continents, all decided to dig down and the rooms they cut look strangely alike.

Bernie Ong has spent years looking closely at those rooms. In this first conversation he takes the question head on: what would it actually take to cut a city out of rock, why does the same shape keep appearing, and what do the tool marks tell you if you stop looking for a mystery and start looking for a method.

We go from Derinkuyu to Borobudur to Sacsayhuaman, examine tool marks with Proto Civilization, and end up somewhere unexpected — with a block of Play-Doh and a very simple demonstration.

With Jeff, Bernie, Cody, and Gerald.

title: Nobody Has Seen Petrie's Labyrinth Since 1889
description:
Petrie drew the inside of the Hawara labyrinth in 1889. Nobody has been back. The chamber filled with groundwater he called "too salt and acrid to put eyes or nose beneath," and the Bahr Selah canal has kept it flooded ever since.

So we did what you can still do: looked at what is above the waterline.

At Hawara, the entrance is mud brick sitting on a megalithic limestone lintel. At Hatun Rumiyoc in Cusco, one wall carries three different builders in three visible bands. In Jerusalem, a single Herodian ashlar in the Western Wall runs 13.6 metres and weighs roughly 517 tonnes. At Baalbek, one quarried block reaches about 1,500 tonnes, and a museum in Interlaken built a model of it ringed with modern cranes, because that is what the comparison takes.

The pattern is not the weight of any one stone. It is the level of work.

title: Predynastic Diorite Vases | Museum Collection · Cairo
description:
Stone vessels by the thousand, some older than the pyramids, turned
from diorite and granite: among the hardest stones on Earth. Wall
thickness, symmetry, lathe-like precision in material that predates
the toolkit credited with making it.

We filmed the cases at the Egyptian Museum in Cairo so you can study
what the placards summarize. Including the tri-lobed schist disc that
has no agreed explanation at all.

Filmed during an @UnchartedX team tour of Egypt.

title: Serapeum of Saqqara with UnchartedX | Fieldwork Walkthrough · Egypt
description:
Twenty-four granite boxes, each up to 70 tons, with lids machined so
precisely they still seal after thousands of years. We went underground
at Saqqara to put our hands on them.

This is our full walkthrough of the Serapeum: the descent from the
plateau, the long gallery, the boxes up close, and a climb inside one
of them. Officially they're bull tombs. The precision is the part
nobody has fully explained.

title: Unfinished Obelisk of Aswan with UnchartedX | Fieldwork · Egypt
description:
Still attached to the bedrock: a 1,000-ton obelisk, abandoned
mid-extraction when cracks appeared. The quarry preserves the entire
workflow: the trench channels, the scoop marks, the test cuts.

We walked the quarry with the UnchartedX team and got close to the
tool marks that fuel one of Egyptology's most practical debates: what
actually cut this granite?

title: The Osireion | Fieldwork Walkthrough · Egypt with UnchartedX
description:
The Osireion sits sunken behind the Temple of Seti I at Abydos:
massive granite blocks in a style that looks nothing like the temple
above it, half-submerged in groundwater, and one of the most debated
monuments in Egypt.

This is our full walkthrough, the way you actually reach it: starting
at the top near the modern town, past the Seti temple complex, and
down to the megalithic core. Red granite lintels, cyclopean pillars,
and joins that raise the questions the guidebooks skip.

Filmed during an @UnchartedX  team tour of Egypt.

title: 60 Metres Under Cappadocia: Walking Inside Derinkuyu Underground City
description:
We walked 60 meters down into Derinkuyu: an underground city carved 18
levels deep beneath Cappadocia, built to shelter 20,000 people with
their livestock and food stores.

This is our full walkthrough: the rolling stone doors, the ventilation
shafts that still breathe, the wells, the stables, and the cruciform
church on the lowest level. Filmed on site, unscripted, the way we
found it.
